stances.claim: Trillanes' exposé denouncing an alleged P50-million payoff in the procurement of the TRO and writ of preliminary injunction that stopped Binay's suspension shook the CA like an intensity-7 earthquake -- especially painful to Justice Jose C. Reyes Jr. who enjoys a heretofore unblemished reputation

Trillanes should back his attack with some proof -- bribery cases usually have no documents because cash is passed without paper, but a credible witness who has seen the payoff or listened to incriminating conversations can provide valuable leads; the consideration may also be a precious object, promised promotion, complimentary airline ticket, paid medical bill, or compromising photo -- anything that shows the magistrate has been infected by what CJP calls the plague of 'ships': kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship

The Supreme Court, with sole power to discipline members of the judiciary, will welcome some kind of prima facie proof (not necessarily conclusive) to initiate an inquiry; Trillanes' mere say-so with nothing more -- however well-meant -- is not enough, or magistrates will be in constant jeopardy of losing reputation on unsubstantiated allegations

The SC has investigated and penalized members even without formal charges, provided some proof or leads, because the quantum of proof in administrative cases is only 'substantial evidence,' not 'proof beyond reasonable doubt'

The Gregory S. Ong case illustrates: taking cue from a Senate blue ribbon committee inquiry and from an Aries Rufo Rappler article showing a photo of Ong with Sen. Jinggoy Estrada and Janet Lim Napoles, CJ Sereno asked the SC to conduct an investigation motu proprio; retired Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez was directed to look into Ong's link to Napoles and subpoenaed Benhur Luy, Marina Sula, Aries Rufo, and Ong himself

Despite Ong's hearsay objection, Gutierrez held that Luy and Sula testified 'in a candid, straightforward and categorical manner... carried the ring of truth' -- ruling that Ong's act of allowing himself to be Napoles' contact, fixing of the Kevlar case, and accepting money constituted gross misconduct; the SC affirmed and found Ong 'GUILTY of GROSS MISCONDUCT, DISHONESTY and IMPROPRIETY' (capital letters in original), dismissed him from service with forfeiture

By the same passion that the SC penalizes erring magistrates, it will not tolerate and will sanction reckless imputations of wrongdoing -- fairness demands that Senator Trillanes produce some proof to back his serious charge of graft; if he cannot, the least he can do is admit his lapse promptly and apologize publicly to the CA justices

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes that the recent 'exposé' of Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV denouncing an alleged P50-million payoff in the procurement of a TRO and writ of preliminary injunction -- which both stopped the suspension of Makati Mayor Jejomar Binay Jr. -- shook the Court of Appeals like an intensity-7 earthquake. The attack was especially painful to Justice Jose C. Reyes Jr., who enjoys a heretofore unblemished reputation for honesty and probity; CA members and employees look up to him as a model of uprightness and competence. If for this reason alone, Trillanes should back his attack with some proof. True, it is quite difficult to secure documents like receipts or checks because in bribery cases cash is usually passed without paper -- but a credible witness will do. Sometimes the consideration is not cash but a precious object or some unfriendly persuasion: a promised promotion, complimentary airline ticket, paid hospital or medical bill, or compromising photo -- anything that shows the magistrate has been infected by what CJP calls the plague of 'ships': kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship. The Supreme Court, vested with sole power to discipline members of the judiciary, will welcome some kind of prima facie proof (not necessarily conclusive) to initiate an inquiry. Trillanes may have been well-intentioned, but his mere say-so with nothing more is not enough -- otherwise magistrates would be in constant jeopardy of losing their reputation on unsubstantiated allegations and could lose their moral ascendancy to dispense justice. The SC has investigated and penalized members of the judiciary even without formal charges, provided some proof or leads of wrongdoing, because the quantum of proof in administrative cases is only 'substantial evidence,' not 'proof beyond reasonable doubt.' The case of Sandiganbayan Justice Gregory S. Ong is a good example. Taking a cue from a Senate blue ribbon committee inquiry on the pork barrel scam indicating prima facie violation of the Judicial Code of Conduct, and from an article by investigative writer Aries Rufo published in Rappler showing a photograph of Ong with Sen. Jinggoy Estrada and Janet Lim Napoles, CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno asked the SC to conduct an investigation motu proprio. After receiving Ong's comment, the Court directed retired Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez to look into Ong's link to Napoles; Gutierrez subpoenaed pork-barrel whistleblowers Benhur Luy and Marina Sula, writer Rufo, and Ong himself. Gutierrez found that Napoles was acquitted by the SBN Fourth Division -- chaired by Ong -- in a case involving the questionable purchase of Kevlar helmets by the PH Marine Corps from five companies owned by Napoles. Luy testified that Napoles 'gave various amounts to different people during the pendency of the case which lasted up to ten years. And before the decision in the Kevlar case was released, she also gave money to respondent (Ong) but she did not mention the amount.' Sula corroborated that Ong visited Napoles' office twice sometime in 2012 and that Napoles would tell her staff that Justice Ong would help her in the Kevlar case. Despite Ong's hearsay objection, Gutierrez held Luy and Sula 'testified in a candid, straightforward and categorical manner... carried the ring of truth,' ruling that Ong's act of allowing himself to be Napoles' contact in the SBN, the fixing of the Kevlar case, and accepting money from her constituted gross misconduct; his picture with an accused in his court 'manifests respondent's disregard of the dictum that propriety and the appearance of propriety are essential to promote public confidence in the integrity of the Judiciary.' Upholding her findings, the SC found Ong 'GUILTY of GROSS MISCONDUCT, DISHONESTY and IMPROPRIETY, all in violation of the New Code of Conduct for the Philippine Judiciary' (capital letters in original) -- dismissed from service with forfeiture of all retirement benefits except accrued leave credits, with prejudice to reemployment in government. CJP details the Ong case to show that the SC, even without direct evidence but with a modicum of proof showing only 'substantial evidence,' has shown willingness to penalize erring magistrates -- and by the same passion will not tolerate, and will sanction, reckless imputations of wrongdoing. In sum, fairness demands that Senator Trillanes produce some proof to back his serious charge of graft. If he cannot, the least he can do is admit his lapse promptly and apologize publicly to the CA justices.
